item.title: USTR Invites Public Comment on Proposed Modifications of the Section 301 Action Regarding Brazil’s Unreasonable Acts, Policies, and Practices
item.description:
USTR Invites Public Comment on Proposed Modifications of the Section 301 Action Regarding Brazil’s Unreasonable Acts, Policies, and Practices myarbrough Wed, 11/25/2026 - 06:40

WASHINGTON – Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer invited public comment on a proposed modification to the Section 301 action regarding Brazil’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices announced on July 15, 2026.

“After over a year of talking, Brazil has made no meaningful progress toward addressing the harmful trade practices that undercut the competitiveness of American farmers, workers, innovators, and businesses,” said Ambassador Greer. “Today’s proposed modification would provide greater leverage to obtain the elimination of Brazil’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices. Specifically, Brazil continues exporting significant amounts of out-of-quota sugar and finished aircraft, which are currently exempt from the action, to the United States. Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table. Consistent with the Section 301 statute, I am also proposing to increase the out-of-quota tariff on sugar imports on a nondiscriminatory basis to prevent a surge of sugar imports from other countries whose market Brazil could backfill. As before, the United States remains open to continuing negotiations with Brazil to bring about long-needed changes to the problems identified in this investigation.”

To be assured of consideration, interested persons should submit requests to appear at the hearing, along with a summary of the testimony, by December 7, 2026. Written comments are due by December 30, 2026. USTR will hold a hearing about the proposed modification on January 14, 2027.

To view the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice, click here.

Background:

Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting U.S. commerce. Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government practices that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. A Section 301(b) investigation examines whether the acts, policies, or practices are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden or restrict U.S. commerce.

At the specific direction of the President, on July 15, 2025, the U.S. Trade Representative (Trade Representative) initiated an investigation under Section 302(b)(1)(a) of the Trade Act regarding the acts, policies, and practices of the Government of Brazil related to digital trade and electronic payment services; unfair, preferential tariffs; anti-corruption enforcement; intellectual property protection; ethanol market access; and illegal deforestation. On July 15, 2025, the Trade Representative requested consultations with Government of Brazil pursuant to Section 303(a) of the Trade Act, which were held on April 15 and 16, 2026. On September 3, 2025, USTR and the Section 301 Committee convened a public hearing regarding the investigation.

On June 1, 2026, the Trade Representative determined that certain of Brazil’s acts, policies, and practices related to these areas are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. As a result of this determination, the Trade Representative proposed responsive action and invited the public to provide written comments by July 1, 2026, on the proposed action. USTR received, reviewed, and analyzed over 360 written comments. On July 6 and July 7, USTR also held a public hearing regarding proposed responsive action in the investigation, at which 77 witnesses testified. On July 20, 2026, the Trade Representative took final action, at President Trump’s direction, by imposing a 25% tariff on certain goods of Brazil.

Since the publication of the July 20, 2026 notice, Brazil has responded by taking legal steps to retaliate against the United States and protect the investigated acts, policies, and practices. Section 307 of the Trade Act of 1974 authorizes the Trade Representative to modify an existing Section 301 action if such action is no longer appropriate. 

Today’s proposal seeks comment on imposing tariffs on two sets of products in order to increase leverage on Brazil to eliminate the acts, policies, and practices found actionable in this investigation. First, USTR is considering increasing duties on imports of certain out-of-quota raw and refined sugar on a nondiscriminatory basis. Sugar is a globally traded, fungible commodity, and Brazil is the global leader in production and export of sugar. Therefore, USTR is proposing this duty on a nondiscriminatory basis to increase the effectiveness of the Section 301 action by preventing Brazilian sugar exporters from backfilling the markets of other sugar producing countries. Second, USTR is considering terminating the current Section 301 action’s exemption for finished aircraft and imposing a 10% ad valorem duty on such imports from Brazil. Finished aircraft are Brazil’s fourth-largest export to the United States.

item.title: USTR Makes Determinations and Proposes Actions in 14 Section 301 Investigations Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors
item.description:
USTR Makes Determinations and Proposes Actions in 14 Section 301 Investigations Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors myarbrough Wed, 11/25/2026 - 06:19

WASHINGTON – Today, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer determined under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 that the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has also published economy-specific reports that support the determinations. The 14 economies covered by today’s determinations are China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. The Trade Representative has not made determinations with respect to Mexico or Norway at this time. 

“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” said Ambassador Greer. “In recognition of this, since 2016, leaders ranging from Donald Trump, to Joe Biden, to Xi Jinping, to Emmanuel Macron have recognized the threat that structural excess capacity and production poses for the global economy. But where successive statements at the G7, G20, WTO and other fora have not resulted in change, President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” 

For the following 14 economies, the U.S. Trade Representative has determined that certain acts, policies, and practices which create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce.

  • Bangladesh: Bangladesh’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to maintain and expand its manufacturing sector, particularly in key sectors; (2) production incentives to promote production and exports; (3) inadequate labor protections; (4) financial repression policies; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Bangladesh and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the ready-made garment and apparel sector.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Cambodia: Cambodia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial policies providing explicit export and manufacturing targets not based on market principles; (2) investment incentives to absorb or expand foreign manufacturing capacity, particularly from non-market economy countries; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; and (4) inadequate labor protections. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Cambodia and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like apparel, solar, and tires.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • China: China’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) long-standing industrial plans and targeting; (2) extensive financial and other support to manufacturers; (3) support to state-owned enterprises on non-commercial terms; (4) extensive forced technology transfer; (5) wide-spread intellectual property theft; (6) inadequate labor protections, including the use of forced labor; (7) lax environmental enforcement; (8) financial repression and currency practices; and (9) encouraging the expansion of capacity and production in third countries. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in China and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in U.S. manufacturing, and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks. This is especially true in the aluminum, automotive, battery, chemical, consumer electronics, glass, machine tool, medical devices, non-ferrous metals, paper, plastics, power equipment, rail, robotics, semiconductors, ship, solar, steel, telecommunications, textiles, tires, and wind sectors.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • European Union: The European Union’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to expand manufacturing; (2) policies to promote production and exports with high volumes of export credit; (3) sustained market access barriers; (4) preferential lending through centralized investment banks that target specific manufacturing sectors; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters to compete in the European Union and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals.  
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • India: India’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to expand manufacturing; (2) inadequate labor protections; (3) financial repression policies; (4) sustained market access barriers; and (5) failed to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in India and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like health (pharmaceuticals and medical devices), steel, solar, and information and communications technology (ICT). 
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Indonesia: Indonesia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) government industrial policies to promote production and export; (2) inadequate labor laws, conditions, and enforcement; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; (4) financial repression; and (5) sector-specific acts, policies, and practices, such as “downstreaming”. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Indonesia and third country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like textiles and apparel, mining and metals production, and renewable energy.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Japan: Japan’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans and strategies; (2) financial repression; (3) household investment promotion; (4) support for unprofitable firms; (5) inadequate labor protections; (6) financial support for the auto, steel, semiconductor, and optical fiber industries; and (7) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Japan and third-country markets, (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector, and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, steel, semiconductors, and optical fiber.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Republic of Korea: Korea’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and sectoral plans to maintain and expand manufacturing; (2) preferential lending through state-owned banks; and (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Korea and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, semiconductor, and petrochemicals. 
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Malaysia: Malaysia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and sectoral plans to promote production and exports; (2) preferential capital through national funding vehicles that target manufacturing; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; and (4) inadequate labor protections. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Malaysia and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like information and communication technology and automotive.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Singapore: Singapore’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans; (2) financial repression; (3) savings promotion policies that suppress domestic consumption; (4) inadequate labor protections; (5) financial support for key sectors; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Singapore and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like electronics and semiconductors, health, and petrochemicals.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Switzerland: Switzerland’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) suppressing the appreciation of its currency below the level that would otherwise prevail under market conditions; (2) supporting its pharmaceutical sector via extensive public investment and fiscal incentives; (3) reducing a major production cost—electricity—for its steel producers; and (4) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Switzerland and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in U.S. manufacturing; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the pharmaceutical, steel, and chemicals sectors.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Taiwan: Taiwan’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) the recurring use of industrial and economic plans to support the manufacturing sector, particularly high-technology manufacturing; (2) legislation that incentivizes and provides support for the architecture of its industrial ecosystem; (3) state-directed and supported research and development; (4) state-directed and industrial clustering to support industry; (5) various financing mechanisms to support industry; (6) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports from non-market economies; (7) practices that equate to financial repression; (8) past purchases of U.S.-sanctioned Russian feedstock; and (9) inadequate protection of labor rights. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Taiwan and third country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like the electronics, semiconductor, and telecommunications sectors.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Thailand: Thailand’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and economic plans that target manufacturing and export; (2) sustained market access barriers; (3) preferential lending and other government support to industry; (4) inadequate labor protections; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Thailand and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the electronics, automobile, machinery, and electrical equipment sectors.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.
  • Vietnam: Vietnam’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) government industrial plans and its state planning system; (2) its land planning system; (3) inadequate labor laws, conditions, and enforcement; (4) financial repression; (5) allocation of financial capital to priority sectors; (6) price regulation; (7) encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investment from other non-market economies; (8) encouragement of or failure to address imports from other non-market economies; (9) encouragement of or failure to address transshipment from other non-market economies; and (10) sector-specific acts, policies, and practices.  These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Vietnam and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on other NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like textiles, apparel, and footwear; shipbuilding; cement; and information and communications technology.
    • Read USTR’s Report here.

As a result of these determinations, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed responsive action in each investigation for public comment. Specifically, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed additional tariffs on the following investigated economies except for certain products identified in the annexes of the respective Federal Register notices.

  • Bangladesh: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Bangladesh of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Bangladesh on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States of American and the People’s Republic of Bangladesh on Reciprocal Trade.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Cambodia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Cambodia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Cambodia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Cambodia on Reciprocal Trade.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • China: The Trade Representative proposes appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20 percent, net of the rate of duty applied to the good under the Section 301 investigation related to the prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor, on goods of China not identified in the annexes to the relevant Federal Register notice and up to 10 percent tariffs on goods identified in Annex A to the Federal Register notice with exemptions for certain goods identified in Annex B to the Federal Register notice. The products in Annex B are products on the U.S. Imports List of the U.S.-China Board of Trade “30-For-30” Lists of Products Recommended for Reduced Tariff Treatment. This proposal accounts for the commitments and 20 percent tariff rate announced as part of the Kuala Lumpur Joint Arrangement reached by President Trump and President Xi on October 30, 2025.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • European Union: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying on all goods of the EU a tariff rate of 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with the EU on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the United States-European Union Framework Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • India: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices would include applying tariffs of up to 25 percent on all goods of India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions, or were India to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of India, a tariff rate of 17 percent. 
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Indonesia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Indonesia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Indonesia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Indonesia on Reciprocal Trade.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Japan: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying on all goods of Japan tariffs of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain products. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Japan on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the framework agreement between the United States and Japan.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Republic of Korea: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Korea of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Korea on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Korea Strategic Trade and Investment Deal.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Malaysia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Malaysia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Malaysia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Malaysia on Reciprocal Trade.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Singapore: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Singapore, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider adjusting the tariff rate applied to each good to 10 percent to account for any commitments in the event that Singapore were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States, or conclude other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Singapore.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Switzerland: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices proposes to consider applying on all goods of Switzerland tariffs of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Switzerland on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in United States-Switzerland-Liechtenstein Framework Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Taiwan: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Taiwan of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain products. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Taiwan on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the U.S.- Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Thailand: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Thailand of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Thailand on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Framework for an Agreement between the United States and Thailand on Reciprocal Trade.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.
  • Vietnam: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 35 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Vietnam, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; or the commitments and a tariff rate of 20 percent, were Vietnam to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Vietnam.
    • Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here.

To be assured of consideration, interested persons should submit requests to appear at the hearings, along with a summary of testimony by January 5, 2027. Written comments are due by January 5, 2027. USTR will hold hearings about the proposed actions in these investigations on January 25, 2027, continuing as appropriate.

Background:

Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting U.S. commerce. Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government practices that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Under Section 302(b) of the Trade Act, the United States Trade Representative may self-initiate an investigation under Section 301.

On March 11, 2026, the United States Trade Representative initiated investigations into the acts, policies, and practices of various economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors. The 16 economies subject to these investigations are: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan, and India.

Pursuant to Section 304(b)(1)(A) of the Trade Act, USTR provided the public and interested persons with opportunities to present their views through a public comment process and through a public hearing. USTR received testimony of nearly 140 witnesses and 1,070 comments in response to the initiation notice and pertaining to all 16 investigated economies.

Today, the U.S. Trade Representative determined, in each of 14 investigations, that the acts, policies, and practices of China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act.

item.title: United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Polygroup Industrias México
item.description:
United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Polygroup Industrias México pbrouillette Thu, 11/19/2026 - 16:12

WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative has invoked the Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) to review whether workers at Polygroup Industrias México, S.A. de C.V. (Polygroup), located in Chihuahua, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The United States has suspended liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Polygroup facility, which manufactures plastic products, including Christmas products and swimming and wading pools.

Background

The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On October 20, 2026, the ILC received an RRM petition from a Mexican union, the Sindicato de Trabajadores de la Industria Química en General, Farmacéutica, Medicamentos, Similares y Conexos de la República Mexicana, and 11 Polygroup workers. The petition alleges that Polygroup is violating its workers’ right to freedom of association and collective bargaining, including by interfering with union activity and by threatening to fire workers in retaliation for union activity. The ILC reviews within 30 days any RRM petition that it receives, and the accompanying information.

After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms under the USMCA. As a result, the Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico under Annex 31-A of the USMCA that Mexico review whether workers at Polygroup are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review. The Trade Representative has also directed the Secretary of the Treasury to suspend liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from Polygroup.

A copy of the request for review can be found here.

A copy of the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury can be found here.

Information about previous requests can be found here.

item.title: Ambassador Greer Pens Letter to the Editor of the Wall Street Journal on how Tariffs are Advancing Americans’ Long-Term Prosperity
item.description:
Ambassador Greer Pens Letter to the Editor of the Wall Street Journal on how Tariffs are Advancing Americans’ Long-Term Prosperity pbrouillette Mon, 11/16/2026 - 09:58

WASHINGTON — This week, Ambassador Jamieson Greer penned a letter to the editor of the Wall Street Journal to challenge the claims made in “How Do You Like Those Tariffs Now.” In the letter, Ambassador Greer uses hard data to dismantle the author’s false assertions and details how President Trump is using tariffs and trade deals to advance the long-term prosperity of American farmers, workers, and manufacturers.

Read Ambassador Greer's full letter to the Wall Street Journal below.

In his op-ed “How Do You Like Those Tariffs Now?” (Nov. 11), David Hebert asserts that economists’ predictions about tariffs came true: “Americans would pay them, trading partners would retaliate, and bullying our allies would backfire.” The data tell a different story on each of these points.

The first point—that American consumers bore the brunt of the tariffs—doesn’t hold up to scrutiny. Caroline Freund of the University of California San Diego published a paper in July concluding that foreign exporters absorbed roughly 40% to 50% of the 2025 U.S. tariff increases through lower export prices, “much more than earlier studies suggested.” Importers of record, typically companies, covered much of the rest. Preston Caldwell, chief U.S. economist at Morningstar, told the Journal last year that “U.S. firms are still footing most of the tariff bill, having yet to pass more than a fraction of the tariff cost on to consumers.”

Nor did the tariffs trigger sweeping global retaliation. While the Trump administration put tariffs on countries all around the world, only two attempted direct retaliation: China and Canada. But in both cases, these countries eventually rolled back some of their retaliatory measures while the U.S. maintained most of its new tariffs. China has resumed buying U.S. soybeans, easing China’s leverage over U.S. farmers.

As for Mr. Hebert’s argument about “backfiring,” 19 U.S. trading partners, accounting for nearly 40% of global gross domestic product, signed deals with us. In these agreements, the U.S. agreed to impose a lower tariff rate in exchange for our trading partners’ resolution of longstanding tariff and nontariff barriers—a prize free-trade fundamentalists have sought for decades. But don’t take our word for it; workers, farmers and industry leaders have praised President Trump’s deals that open foreign markets while expanding domestic jobs and investment.

The U.S. has exported over $300 billion in goods and services every month this year, breaking records. We are in the tenth month of a manufacturing expansion. The economy is close to full employment. While Europe’s economic growth is sluggish and Canada’s unemployment rate rose to 6.7% in October, the U.S. is the most dynamic economy in the Group of Seven. So, yes, we like these tariffs very much.

item.title: United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Industrias FG
item.description:
United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Industrias FG pbrouillette Fri, 11/13/2026 - 16:27

WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative has invoked the Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) to review whether workers at a facility operated by Industrias FG, S.A. de C.V. (the Facility), located in Morelos, Mexico, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The United States has suspended liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Facility, which manufactures polyurethane hydraulic seals used in machinery that includes pistons.

Background

The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On October 13, 2026, the ILC received a RRM petition from the Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadoras y Trabajadores de Industrias y Servicios “Ricardo Flores Magón,” a Mexican labor union. The petition alleges that the Facility has violated workers’ right to freedom of association and collective bargaining by coercing workers to support a union of the company’s choice; refusing to bargain with the duly authorized union; discriminating against workers due to their union activity, including through retaliatory dismissals; and otherwise interfering with workers’ union activities, including through interrogations, harassment, threats and misinformation. The ILC reviews within 30 days any RRM petition that it receives and accompanying information.

After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms under the USMCA. As a result, the Trade Representative has submitted a request under Annex 31-A of the USMCA that Mexico review whether workers at the Facility are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Trade Representative has also directed the Secretary of the Treasury to suspend liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Facility.

Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review.

A copy of the request for review can be found here.

A copy of the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury can be found here.

During the call, Ambassador Greer emphasized the critical importance of China taking concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals. WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative has invoked the Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) to review whether workers at Madobox, S.A. de C.V. (Madobox), located in the city of Uruapan in the state of Michoacán, Mexico, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The U.S. request for review follows an RRM petition received from a Mexican labor union alleging that Madobox is interfering with union activity at the facility. The United States has suspended liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Madobox facility, which produces boxes for commercial use.

Background

The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On September 30, 2026, the Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores y Empleados de la Industria del Comercio, Alimenticia, Textil, Automotriz, Metalúrgica, Servicios y Distribución “Generalísimo José María Morelos y Pavón”—a Mexican labor union affiliated with the Confederacion Central Nacional (COCENA)—filed a Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) petition alleging a denial of rights at Madobox. The petition alleges that Madobox is interfering with union activity at the facility, including by unlawfully arranging a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) that was negotiated without workers, by coercing and misinforming workers about the CBA and their union rights, and by unlawfully dismissing workers in retaliation for union activity. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days.

After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms under the USMCA. As a result, the Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico under Annex 31-A of the USMCA that Mexico review whether workers at Madobox are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Trade Representative has also directed the Secretary of the Treasury to suspend liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from Madobox.  

Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review.

item.title: United States and Mexico Announce Memorandum of Understanding at Industrias Tecnos Facility
item.description:
United States and Mexico Announce Memorandum of Understanding at Industrias Tecnos Facility pbrouillette Mon, 11/02/2026 - 15:13

WASHINGTON — The United States and Mexico announced today a memorandum of understanding regarding denial of rights concerns at the Industrias Tecnos, S.A. de C.V. (Industrias Tecnos or the company) facility located in Cuernavaca, Morelos, Mexico, where the company manufactures small arms ammunition.  

The memorandum of understanding details a plan to remedy violations of Mexican law at the facility and includes actions aimed at ensuring freedom of association and collective bargaining rights are protected at the facility moving forward.

Under the terms of the memorandum of understanding, the Government of Mexico (Mexico) will ensure that Industrias Tecnos takes various remedial actions, including to:

  • Verify proper compensation for dismissed workers as required by Mexican law, for any wages or benefits those workers did not receive as a result of unlawful dismissals;
  • Implement and train all company personnel on a neutrality statement and guidelines related to the freedom of association and collective bargaining, including a zero-tolerance policy for violations, and commit to additional retraining as needed; 
  • Install and publicize a complaint mechanism through which workers can report violations of their rights and breaches of company policies anonymously and confidentially; and
  • Maintain on the company website and in any internal communications platform the neutrality statement and guidelines, training materials, and information about complaint mechanisms maintained by the company and Mexico, such that the information is easily accessible to workers.

Under the terms of the memorandum of understanding, Mexico will, among other actions:

  • Review and verify determinations made in relation to dismissed workers identified by the United States to ensure outcomes were effectuated in accordance with Mexican law;
  • Monitor the facility with regard to the obligations of the memorandum of understanding and compliance with Mexican laws related to freedom of association and collective bargaining; 
  • Conduct in-person training that is structured to ensure all workers understand their right to freedom of association and collective bargaining and how to exercise it;
  • Conduct separate workers’ rights training for supervisors, human resources and labor relations personnel, and other high-level and “trusted” officials; and
  • Maintain a direct email address, reporting platform, and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of freedom of association and collective bargaining rights, and timely investigate any allegations.

The United States and Mexico agreed to establish a deadline of October 15, 2026, to complete the actions listed in the memorandum of understanding.

Background

The United States Trade Representative and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On May 23, 2024, the ILC received a Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) petition from Sindicato Independiente de Trabajadores y Empleados, Transporte, Carga y Descarga, Exploración y Explotación de Minerales Básicos, Productos Metálicos, Similares y Conexos de la República Mexicana (Sindicato Metálico), a Mexican labor union. The petition alleged an ongoing Denial of Rights by Industrias Tecnos at its facility in Morelos, Mexico. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms.    

As a result, on June 24, 2024, the United States submitted a request that Mexico review the matter, and Mexico thereafter agreed to conduct a review. After Mexico issued a report finding no Denial of Rights at the facility, the United States requested the establishment of a panel pursuant to Article 31-A.5.1(a) of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.  

Read the full memorandum of understanding here.
